questions.subtopic: 3D1 Qualities of good results communication. A board summary with no support behind its rating
questions.question: The chief audit executive reviews a one-page board summary of a port's cargo-scanning engagement: plain language, figures traced, but no findings or reasons behind its unsatisfactory rating. Which quality does the summary most lack?
questions.key_concept: Complete means enough relevant, reliable and sufficient support for a reader to reach the auditors' conclusion; plain wording alone does not supply it.
questions.pre_read: Match the flaw to the fix it needs: correct a fact, explain a term, add support or cut padding.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.2 describes a complete communication as one with enough relevant, reliable and sufficient support that its reader would reach the auditors' conclusion. A rating with no findings or reasons behind it fails that; a board version may carry less detail, never no support. Clear, the closest choice, asks whether readers can follow the text, and this summary is plain and free of jargon. Standard 15.1 requires completeness of final communications.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Standard 11.2 links supporting detail to clarity too, but clear asks whether the text is logical and easy to follow, which this is; the gap is completeness.
wrong_explanations.B: Accurate concerns errors and distortions; the figures trace to the workpapers, and nothing in the summary is wrong, only unsupported.
wrong_explanations.D: Concise means no padding or repetition; a one-page summary is not padded, and concision never justifies dropping the support a conclusion needs.

tips: Eliminate: B, because every figure traces to the workpapers, and D, because a one-page summary has no padding to cut.
Final two: C beats A because the text is easy to follow; what is missing is the support a reader needs to reach the same rating.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, name the quality by the fix it needs: add support (complete), explain terms (clear), cut padding (concise), correct facts (accurate).
questions.framework_ref: Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 11.2 Effective Communication; Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 15.1 Final Engagement Communication

Bullet 3D1b, seat: the chief audit executive reviewing a board version before approval. Doubt logged: Standard 11.2 also says supporting details improve clarity, so the stem states the summary is plain and jargon-free and has no findings or reasons behind its rating (fix pass, 25 Nov 2026). Nearest items: cia1_d2_036 (a shorter board version keeps every finding: an honesty lesson), cia1_d2_069 (clear means the reader's own terms). questions.subtopic: 3D1 Qualities of good results communication. What the chief audit executive must set up
questions.question: A cocoa exporter's audit committee tells the chief audit executive (CAE) that three regional teams' reports differ in structure and tone; no written guidance exists. Which step is the CAE most clearly required to take?

options.A: Set a style guide, template and review steps for all teams.
options.B: Add report-quality measures to the quality assurance program.
options.C: Give every auditor training in report writing and presenting.
options.D: Ask the audit committee to approve one report template.

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive must establish communication methodologies for the whole function; general writing training and communication measures are optional additions.
questions.pre_read: Sort each option into what a standard requires of the chief audit executive and what it only permits.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.2 requires the chief audit executive to establish and implement methodologies that promote the seven qualities, and its considerations name style guides, procedures and supervisory review. With no written guidance, setting one for every team meets that requirement. Writing and presentation training, the closest choice, is a may under Standard 11.2; Standard 9.3's must is training on the methodologies, which cannot come before they exist.

wrong_explanations.B: Communication measures in the quality program are a may under Standard 11.2; they track results once a method exists rather than creating one.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: writing and presentation training is a may under Standard 11.2; Standard 9.3 requires training on the methodologies, which must exist first, so training cannot replace setting one.
wrong_explanations.D: The chief audit executive sets the function's methodologies, shaped by stakeholder expectations; the Standards give the board no approval role over report templates (Standards 9.3, 11.2).

tips: Eliminate: B, because quality-program measures are optional and track a method rather than create one, and D, because the chief audit executive, not the board, sets methodologies.
Final two: A beats C because a method must exist before auditors can be trained on it, as Standard 9.3 requires; general writing training is only a may under Standard 11.2.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, setting the function's methodologies and training auditors on them are musts; extra writing courses and communication measures are mays.

questions.subtopic: 3D2 Writing the final engagement communication. A step missed and no time to redo it
questions.question: Approving an assurance engagement's final communication at a grain trader, the chief audit executive (CAE) learns planning never considered fraud risks; a regulator's deadline rules out redoing it. What is the CAE's best course?

options.A: Omit the conformance statement and add nothing else to the report.
options.B: Keep the conformance statement and fix the gap in later engagements.
options.C: Omit the statement; brief the board on the gap, reason and impact.
options.D: Omit the statement; state the gap, reason and impact in the report.

questions.key_concept: An engagement that did not conform must disclose, in its final communication, the standard not met, the reason and the impact on its results.
questions.pre_read: Ask two things: may the conformance statement stay, and what must the final communication itself say about a missed requirement?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 15.1 supports a conformance statement only when supervision and the quality program back it, so it goes. It then requires the final engagement communication itself to disclose the standard not met, here Standard 13.2's fraud-risk step, the reasons and the impact on findings and conclusions. Briefing the board, the closest choice, may also suit the chief audit executive's reporting, but it does not replace disclosure to the report's readers.

wrong_explanations.A: Dropping the statement is right, but silence is not: Standard 15.1 requires the final communication to disclose a nonconformance with its standard, reason and impact.
wrong_explanations.B: The statement is used only when supervision and the quality program support it (Standard 15.1); a known gap in this engagement rules it out, whatever later work fixes.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the board may need to hear of it, but Standard 15.1 places the disclosure in the final engagement communication, where every reader of the results sees it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the statement needs support from supervision and the quality program, and A, because a nonconformance must be disclosed, not merely left unstated.
Final two: D beats C because Standard 15.1 puts the standard, reason and impact in the final communication itself, not only in a briefing to the board.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, the conformance statement is a should used only with support; disclosing a nonconformance in the final communication is the must.

questions.subtopic: 3D2 Writing the final engagement communication. What an advisory report must carry
questions.question: The chief audit executive is approving an advisory engagement's final communication on a shipyard's new supplier-onboarding design; the draft holds recommendations only. Which of the following additions is most clearly required?

options.A: Each finding with its significance and its priority ranking.
options.B: A statement of the objectives, scope and conclusions.
options.C: An explanation of any scope limitations and their effect.
options.D: A conclusion on governance, risk management and control effectiveness.

questions.key_concept: Every final communication states objectives, scope and conclusions; prioritized findings, scope limitations and an effectiveness conclusion are added for assurance work.
questions.pre_read: First ask what kind of engagement this was; then separate what every final communication carries from what only assurance reports add.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 15.1 requires every final communication, advisory ones included, to state the engagement's objectives, scope and conclusions, plus any recommendations or action plans. A conclusion on the effectiveness of governance, risk management and control, the closest choice, is one of three items Standard 15.1 adds only for assurance engagements, with prioritized findings and scope limitations. For advisory work, Standard 14.5 says the conclusions should align with the agreed objectives and scope.

wrong_explanations.A: Findings with their significance and priority are an assurance-only requirement in Standard 15.1, not one for an advisory engagement's final communication.
wrong_explanations.C: Standard 15.1 lists an explanation of scope limitations among the three additions for assurance engagements only; an advisory final communication must carry the core: objectives, scope and conclusions.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: an effectiveness conclusion is required in assurance final communications only (Standard 15.1); an advisory conclusion should match the agreed objectives and scope (Standard 14.5).

tips: Eliminate: A, because prioritized findings are an assurance-only requirement, and C, because explaining scope limitations is required of assurance reports, not advisory ones.
Final two: B beats D because objectives, scope and conclusions are required for every engagement, while an effectiveness conclusion is required only for assurance work.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about report contents, check the engagement type first: assurance adds three items to the core that every final communication carries.

questions.subtopic: 3D2 Writing the final engagement communication. Owners and dates left for the tracker
questions.question: Management agreed actions, none yet begun, from a phosphate miner's maintenance engagement but wants owners and dates entered in the tracker later. What must the chief audit executive most clearly ensure before approving the report?

options.A: The tracker holds each owner and date before the first follow-up.
options.B: The report names the follow-up auditor as each action's owner.
options.C: The report names each action's owner and planned completion date.
options.D: The report acknowledges any actions management has already completed.

questions.key_concept: The final communication itself names who will address each finding and the planned completion date; the tracker records them later and never replaces them.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the owners and dates must first appear: in the final communication, or only in later follow-up records.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 15.1 requires the final communication to name who will deal with each finding and the date by which the action is planned. Leaving them for the tracking system, the closest choice, would issue a report without a required part; the tracker under Standard 15.2 follows actions after issue and draws on what the report set. Management owns the actions, so the owners named are managers, not internal auditors.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the tracker records owners and dates for follow-up (Standard 15.2), but Standard 15.1 requires them in the final communication itself, before issue.
wrong_explanations.B: Management owns and implements actions (Standard 14.4); internal auditors confirm them later. Naming an auditor as owner puts internal audit in management's role.
wrong_explanations.D: Acknowledging actions already taken is a Standard 15.1 must only when management has started or finished them before issue; here actions are only agreed, and owners and dates are missing.

tips: Eliminate: B, because management, not internal audit, owns the actions, and D, because acknowledging completed actions applies only when management has already acted, which it has not.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 15.1 requires owners and dates in the final communication; the tracking system follows them afterward.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, when a Standard makes something part of the final communication, a later record such as a tracker never stands in for it.

questions.subtopic: 3D3 Recommendations and management action plans. A dispute that threatens internal audit's access
questions.question: An air-cargo firm's finance chief, part of senior management, disputes a hedging finding, warning the chief audit executive (CAE) of lost treasury access unless the finding is dropped. What must the CAE most clearly do?

options.A: Drop the finding and record the finance chief's objection.
options.B: Work with senior management to settle the dispute first.
options.C: Attach each party's formal statement to the final communication.
options.D: Brief the board on the dispute and the finance chief's threat.

questions.key_concept: When a disagreement with senior management may affect internal audit's ability to do its work, the chief audit executive must give the board the facts.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether this is an ordinary dispute over results or one that threatens the function's ability to work.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 8.1 requires the chief audit executive, when a disagreement with senior management or others could hinder the function in doing its work, to give the board the facts and circumstances so it can decide whether to step in. A threat to cut access does exactly that. Working with senior management, the closest choice, is what Standard 14.4 suggests for an ordinary dispute over results; here senior management is making the threat.

wrong_explanations.A: Results change only for a valid reason, such as new evidence (Standard 13.1); a threat is not one, and dropping the finding would yield to it.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Standard 8.1's considerations do suggest discussing it with senior management so the board hears management's view, but a threat to access must still reach the board, a must.
wrong_explanations.C: Attaching formal statements from each party is an option Standard 14.4 offers for disputes; it records positions but does nothing about the threat to access.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a threat is not a valid reason to change results, and C, because attaching both parties' statements is optional and leaves the threat unaddressed.
Final two: D beats B because a dispute that may affect the function's ability to work must reach the board; talking with senior management may come too, but never in place of it.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about disagreements, ask whether the function's ability to work is at stake; if it is, the board must get the facts.

questions.subtopic: 3D4 Closing communication and report distribution. A significant error found after issue
questions.question: An issued report understated a bus maker's scrap losses, a significant error by board-agreed criteria; it went to the plant manager, operations chief and audit committee. What should the chief audit executive do first?

options.A: Send corrected figures promptly to the audit committee alone.
options.B: Send corrected figures promptly to all three original recipients.
options.C: Send corrected figures promptly to all three and the external auditor.
options.D: Send corrected figures to all three once the error's cause is fixed.

questions.key_concept: A significant error in an issued final communication is corrected promptly for every party who received the original; finding its cause comes alongside, not first.
questions.pre_read: Ask who received the original, how fast the correction must go, and where finding the cause fits.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.4 requires the chief audit executive to send corrected information promptly to everyone who received a final communication containing a significant error, with significance judged on criteria agreed with the board. Waiting until the cause is fixed, the closest choice, reverses the order: the considerations ask the chief audit executive to find the cause and prevent a repeat in addition to correcting, not before it.

wrong_explanations.A: The board oversees internal audit, but the correction must reach every party who received the original, the plant manager and operations chief included (Standard 11.4).
wrong_explanations.C: The correction goes to those who received the original; the external auditor did not, and an outside release first needs legal counsel's or senior management's advice as required (Standard 11.3).
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: finding the error's cause is a should under Standard 11.4, but it does not delay the correction, which must go promptly to every original recipient.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the correction goes to every original recipient, not only the board, and C, because the external auditor never received the original, and an outside release needs advice as required.
Final two: B beats D because the correction must go promptly; finding and fixing the error's cause runs alongside it, not before it.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about a significant error after issue, think: everyone who got the original, promptly, then fix the cause.

questions.subtopic: 3D4 Closing communication and report distribution. A lender asks for a final report
questions.question: A toll-road operator's lending bank asks the chief audit executive (CAE) for the final report on toll-revenue controls; no law or contract requires release, and the charter is silent. What is the CAE's best course?

options.A: Release it to the bank once the CAE approves the recipient list.
options.B: Seek the board's approval before releasing the report.
options.C: Seek advice from legal counsel or senior management first.
options.D: Seek the toll-revenue manager's consent before releasing it.

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive decides who receives final communications, but must seek legal counsel's or senior management's advice, as required, before any outside release.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the recipient is inside or outside the organization, and whether a law already settles the release.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.3 gives the chief audit executive the decision on recipients and adds a must for outside parties: seek the advice of legal counsel, senior management or both, as required, before release, unless laws require or restrict otherwise. No law applies here. Releasing on the chief audit executive's own authority, the closest choice, skips that step; the Standards require no board approval and no consent from the activity's manager.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the chief audit executive does decide recipients (Standard 11.3), but a release outside the organization first needs advice from legal counsel or senior management as required.
wrong_explanations.B: The Standards require advice, not board approval, before an outside release; the board oversees results but does not approve each report's recipients (Standard 11.3).
wrong_explanations.D: The management of the activity under review does not decide who receives internal audit results; the chief audit executive does, after the required advice (Standard 11.3).

tips: Eliminate: B, because an outside release needs advice rather than board approval, and D, because the audited manager does not decide where results go.
Final two: C beats A because the chief audit executive's authority over recipients still requires advice from legal counsel or senior management before an outside release.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, inside the organization the chief audit executive picks recipients; outside it, advice from legal counsel or senior management comes first unless law settles it.

questions.subtopic: 3D5 Residual risk, aggregation and ratings. A conclusion after the rating scale is dropped
questions.question: A food exporter's chief audit executive dropped the audit rating scale; an assurance conclusion then calls cold-storage controls ineffective in two of six areas, silent on four that worked. What is most clearly missing?

options.A: A statement that the other four areas are effective.
options.B: The number of findings at each level of significance.
options.C: Management's signed agreement with the conclusion.
options.D: An overall rating for the activity on a defined scale.

questions.key_concept: An assurance conclusion must judge effectiveness and acknowledge processes that work; a rating scale is an optional way to express that judgment.
questions.pre_read: Separate what every assurance conclusion must contain from tools the methodology may use to express it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.5 requires an assurance conclusion to give the internal auditors' judgment on the effectiveness of governance, risk management or control, acknowledging where processes are effective; silence on four working areas misses that. A rating on a defined scale, the closest choice, is something the chief audit executive's methodology may provide under the considerations; with the scale dropped, nothing requires one.

wrong_explanations.B: A count of findings does not express the overall judgment; the conclusion summarizes the aggregated significance of the findings (Standard 14.5), which a tally cannot.
wrong_explanations.C: The conclusion is the internal auditors' judgment; management may disagree through the established methodology, but its agreement is not a required part (Standards 13.1, 14.5).
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: Standard 14.5's considerations allow a rating scale in the methodology, but it is optional; acknowledging effective processes is the requirement this conclusion misses.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a tally of findings is not a judgment on effectiveness, and C, because the conclusion is the auditors' judgment and needs no management signature.
Final two: A beats D because Standard 14.5 requires acknowledging effective processes, while a rating scale is only a methodology option.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about conclusions, the must is a judgment on effectiveness that credits what works; scales and ratings are tools the methodology may add.

questions.subtopic: 3D6 When management accepts too much risk. Agreement reached with the responsible manager
questions.question: A ferry operator's maintenance head accepted inspection delays beyond the board's tolerance, then agreed with the chief audit executive (CAE) that a plan's interim checks bring risk within tolerance. What is the CAE's best step?

options.A: Track the agreed plan through internal audit's follow-up.
options.B: Report the accepted risk to the board at its next meeting.
options.C: Discuss the accepted risk with senior management before closing it.
options.D: Have the maintenance head sign a formal acceptance of the risk.

questions.key_concept: The Standard 11.5 route runs only while agreement with the responsible management cannot be reached; an agreed updated plan is followed up instead.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether management still accepts the excess risk after the meeting, or has agreed a plan to bring it within tolerance.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.5's considerations have the chief audit executive raise accepted excess risk with the responsible management first, aiming at an updated action plan, and say the standard's requirements apply only when that agreement cannot be reached. Here it was reached, so the plan is confirmed through follow-up under Standard 15.2. Discussing it with senior management, the closest choice, is the required next step only if the head had not agreed.

wrong_explanations.B: The board hears accepted excess risk only if senior management leaves it unresolved (Standard 11.5); this matter was settled at the first step.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Standard 11.5 requires discussion with senior management when agreement with the responsible management fails; here both agree the plan's interim checks bring risk back within tolerance.
wrong_explanations.D: A signed acceptance would record a risk the head is no longer accepting; the agreed plan is what needs tracking and confirmation (Standard 15.2).

tips: Eliminate: B, because the board hears only what senior management leaves unresolved, and D, because the head now plans to act rather than accept the risk.
Final two: A beats C because the Standard 11.5 route continues only when the responsible management will not agree; an agreed plan goes to follow-up.
Exam cue: on CIA risk acceptance questions, read whether agreement was reached: no agreement climbs to senior management, then the board; agreement moves to follow-up.

questions.subtopic: 3D6 When management accepts too much risk. No written risk appetite
questions.question: A family-owned mining firm has no written risk appetite; its site manager accepts gaps in tailings-dam monitoring. Which yardstick should the chief audit executive most rely on to judge whether that risk is unacceptable?

options.A: None until the board and senior management write one down.
options.B: The chief audit executive's own professional view of how much risk is too much.
options.C: The site manager's limits under the delegation schedule.
options.D: What the board and senior management show the firm will accept.

questions.key_concept: The test is the organization's risk appetite or tolerance; with nothing written, the chief audit executive learns it from the board and senior management.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose acceptable level of risk sets the test, and how the chief audit executive learns it when nothing is written down.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.5 measures accepted risk against the organization's risk appetite or risk tolerance, not against any one person's view. Its considerations describe the chief audit executive learning that level through discussions with the board and senior management, stakeholder relationships and audit results, so a written statement is not a precondition. The chief audit executive's own view, the closest choice, feeds the judgment, but the yardstick stays the organization's.

wrong_explanations.A: The considerations have the chief audit executive learn the organization's tolerance through discussions and audit results; the test applies whether or not anyone has written it down (Standard 11.5).
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the chief audit executive's judgment decides whether the level is exceeded, but the level itself is the organization's appetite or tolerance, not a personal comfort (Standard 11.5).
wrong_explanations.C: Standard 11.5 tests against the organization's appetite or tolerance, learned from the board, senior management and audit results; one manager's approval limit only says what that manager may sign.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the test applies whether or not the appetite is written down, and C, because one manager's approval limit does not set the organization's tolerance.
Final two: D beats B because the chief audit executive judges against the organization's acceptable level of risk, learned from the board and senior management, not a personal standard.
Exam cue: on CIA risk acceptance questions, the yardstick is always the organization's appetite or tolerance; the chief audit executive's judgment applies it but never replaces it.

questions.subtopic: 3D7 Following up on action plans. Forty-eight actions and ten days
questions.question: The chief audit executive's team must confirm 48 actions a power utility reports complete, 6 of them on high-rated findings, with ten staff days available. Which of the following follow-up approaches is best?

options.A: Ask all owners, test 6 picked at random, update the tracker.
options.B: Ask all owners, test the 6 high-rated, update the tracker.
options.C: Sample-test all 48 actions, spreading the ten days evenly.
options.D: Ask all owners, close each on written confirmation, update the tracker.

questions.key_concept: Follow-up asks about progress, assesses on a risk basis and updates the tracker, with the effort scaled to each finding's significance.
questions.pre_read: Recall the three follow-up steps, then decide how deep each action's confirmation should go, given its finding's significance.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 15.2 requires a follow-up methodology that inquires about progress, performs follow-up assessments on a risk basis and updates a tracking system, with the extent set by each finding's significance; completed actions may be assessed selectively. Asking every owner, testing the six high-rated actions and updating the tracker does all three. Closing all 48 on written confirmations, the closest choice, gives the high-rated actions no more scrutiny than the rest.

wrong_explanations.A: All three steps appear, but a random pick ignores significance: Standard 15.2 requires follow-up assessments on a risk basis, so the six high-rated actions are the ones to test.
wrong_explanations.C: Testing every action spreads ten days thinly and ignores significance; Standard 15.2 lets follow-up assessments be selective, weighted toward the high-rated findings.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: inquiry and tracking are required steps, but closing high-rated actions on owners' word alone ignores the must to scale effort to significance (Standard 15.2).

tips: Eliminate: C, because spreading tests evenly does not scale effort to significance, and A, because random picks may skip the high-rated actions that most need assessing.
Final two: B beats D because Standard 15.2 scales follow-up to significance: the six high-rated actions need assessment, not just the owner's word.
Exam cue: on CIA follow-up questions, look for all three steps (inquire, assess on a risk basis, track), with testing weighted to the most significant findings.

questions.subtopic: 3D8 Escalating actions that were not completed. A past-due action and the owner's reason
questions.question: An internal auditor finds a hotel group's guest-data fix four months past due; its owner, the IT manager, blames a vendor delay, with no new date. What is the internal auditor's best course?

options.A: Mark it past due for the chief audit executive's quarterly review.
options.B: Document the reason and report it to the audit committee chair.
options.C: Ask the IT director to set and enforce a new completion date.
options.D: Document the reason and discuss it with the chief audit executive.

questions.key_concept: When an action misses its date, internal auditors must obtain and document management's explanation and discuss it with the chief audit executive.
questions.pre_read: Ask what Standard 15.2 requires of the follow-up auditor once a date is missed, before anyone judges risk acceptance.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 15.2 requires internal auditors, when management has not progressed by the agreed dates, to obtain and document management's explanation and discuss the issue with the chief audit executive, who then judges whether risk beyond tolerance has been accepted. Marking it past due for a quarterly review, the closest choice, keeps the tracker current but supplies neither the documented explanation nor the discussion.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a past-due flag reaches the chief audit executive, but Standard 15.2 requires management's explanation documented and discussed; a flag awaiting a review does neither.
wrong_explanations.B: Documenting the reason is right, but it goes to the chief audit executive, who judges whether delay means accepted risk and any escalation (Standards 15.2, 11.5).
wrong_explanations.C: Management owns its action plan and dates; internal audit does not set or enforce them, and going to a director bypasses the chief audit executive.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the documented reason goes to the chief audit executive, who judges any escalation, and C, because management owns its dates and actions.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 15.2 requires the auditor to document management's explanation and discuss it with the chief audit executive; a past-due flag does neither.
Exam cue: on CIA follow-up questions, a missed date triggers two auditor steps: document management's explanation, then take it to the chief audit executive.

questions.subtopic: 3D8 Escalating actions that were not completed. The chief audit executive's call on a repeated delay
questions.question: An internal auditor documents why a ceramics maker's kiln-safety action has missed its date twice and brings it to the chief audit executive (CAE). What is the CAE's primary responsibility at this point?

options.A: Set a firm new deadline and require the plant to meet it.
options.B: Have the auditor keep tracking each new date the plant sets.
options.C: Judge whether the delay shows management accepting excess risk.
options.D: Report the delay to the board as risk beyond its tolerance.

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive determines whether delay or inaction means senior management has accepted risk beyond tolerance; escalation follows only from that judgment.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose judgment Standard 15.2 calls for once the auditor brings a documented delay, and what that judgment decides.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 15.2 makes the chief audit executive responsible for determining whether delay or inaction by senior management amounts to accepting risk beyond the risk tolerance. That judgment decides whether the Standard 11.5 route starts. Continuing to track new dates, the closest choice, keeps the record current, but a repeated slip on a safety action calls for the judgment, not only more tracking.

wrong_explanations.A: Management owns its action plan and dates; the chief audit executive may agree an updated plan with management but does not order one (Standards 14.4, 11.5).
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: tracking continues, but Standard 15.2 requires the chief audit executive to judge whether repeated delay amounts to accepting risk, not to log new dates indefinitely.
wrong_explanations.D: Escalation follows the chief audit executive's judgment and runs through senior management before the board (Standards 15.2, 11.5); labeling it accepted risk and going straight to the board skips both.

tips: Eliminate: A, because management owns its dates and actions, and D, because the board comes after the chief audit executive's judgment and senior management.
Final two: C beats B because Standard 15.2 gives the chief audit executive the duty to judge whether delay means accepted risk; tracking alone never makes that call.
Exam cue: on CIA escalation questions, auditors document and report the delay; the chief audit executive judges whether it is accepted risk; only then does escalation begin.

questions.subtopic: 3D3 Recommendations and management action plans. A plan that repairs only the items found
questions.question: Approving a draft, the chief audit executive (CAE) sees a distributor's plan reprice 40 invoices and retrain clerks; the root cause agreed with management: any clerk can override prices. What is the CAE's best step?

options.A: Approve it, and check in follow-up whether overrides have stopped.
options.B: Have the team take the plan back to management before approval.
options.C: Write an override block into the report as management's action.
options.D: Raise the plan with senior management as risk beyond tolerance.

questions.key_concept: A plan is judged against the root cause agreed with management; one that repairs the items found but leaves the cause goes back for discussion.
questions.pre_read: Ask which step of the plan changes why prices went wrong, and who revises a plan that falls short.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.3 has internal auditors identify root causes with management where possible; Standard 14.4 aims actions at the root cause, and its considerations have auditors evaluate, with management, whether a plan handles the risk within tolerance. Repricing and retraining leave any clerk free to override prices, so the team raises this with management, which revises its plan. Approving and checking later, the closest choice, confirms a plan that misses the cause.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: follow-up confirms that agreed actions were carried out (Standard 15.2); it cannot repair a plan that never touches the overrides where the cause lies.
wrong_explanations.C: Management owns and implements its plan (Standard 14.4). Writing internal audit's own fix in as management's action takes the plan over; a recommendation is first discussed with management.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 11.5's route starts when the chief audit executive concludes management accepted risk beyond appetite or tolerance. Nobody has told management its plan misses the cause.

tips: Eliminate: C, because internal audit does not write its own fix into management's plan, and D, because management has refused nothing, so the risk acceptance route has not begun.
Final two: B beats A because Standard 14.4 aims actions at the root cause and its considerations have auditors weigh plans with management; follow-up confirms only what was agreed.
Exam cue: on CIA action plan questions, match each step to the agreed root cause; correcting the items found treats the symptom, and the plan goes back to management.

questions.subtopic: 3D1 Qualities of good results communication. A blaming word in a well-supported draft
questions.question: The chief audit executive reviews a draft on a fishery's quota checks: every fact is supported, recommendations invite joint fixes, but one finding calls dock supervisors 'negligent'. Which quality does the draft most lack?
questions.key_concept: Objective means impartial and balanced, free of wording a reader could take as biased; a blaming label breaks it even when every fact is right.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the draft says from how it labels people, and recall which quality the Standard ties to biased terms.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.2's considerations describe objective communication as fair and even-handed, resting on all the relevant facts, and ask internal auditors to steer clear of wording a reader could take as biased. Calling supervisors 'negligent' passes judgment on people where a neutral account of the missed checks would serve. Constructive, the closest choice, concerns a cooperative, helpful tone aimed at improvement, which the jointly framed recommendations already show. Standard 15.1 requires all seven qualities.

wrong_explanations.A: Clear means logical and easily understood, in the organization's own terms, with uncommon terms defined. 'Negligent' is plain to any reader; the problem is bias, not understanding.
wrong_explanations.B: Concise means free of unnecessary detail and repetition. One loaded word is not padding; the flaw lies in what the word implies, not in the draft's length.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: constructive is a helpful, cooperative tone that supports improvement, which the recommendations already show; Standard 11.2 places biased terms under objective.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a plain word every reader understands meets clear, and B, because one word is neither padding nor repetition.
Final two: D beats C because Standard 11.2 puts wording a reader could take as biased under objective; constructive concerns the helpful tone of the whole message.
Exam cue: on CIA communication questions, a wrong fact breaks accurate, one-sided or blaming wording breaks objective, padding breaks concise, and jargon breaks clear.

questions.subtopic: 3D7 Following up on action plans. Plans management wrote itself
questions.question: The chief audit executive's team plans follow-up for a pharmacy engagement: six actions came from internal audit's recommendations, four from the head pharmacist's own plans, most low-rated. Which approach is best?

options.A: Confirm all ten under the function's usual follow-up method.
options.B: Confirm the six recommendations; the pharmacist self-reports the four plans.
options.C: Retest all ten in full before any of them is closed.
options.D: Confirm the six; the risk function confirms the four plans.

questions.key_concept: Internal auditors confirm that management's own action plans, as well as their recommendations, are implemented under the function's follow-up methodology; management still implements.
questions.pre_read: Read who wrote each action, then check whether Standard 15.2's follow-up duty, and its scaling to significance, depend on that.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 15.2 requires internal auditors to confirm implementation of their own recommendations and of the action plans management writes, under an established methodology. Who drafted an action does not change the duty, and management still carries every action out. Leaving the pharmacist's four plans to self-reporting, the closest choice, treats follow-up as management's job alone, which the Standard rules out.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: recommendations are covered, but Standard 15.2 names management's action plans too; management implements them, and internal auditors confirm them whoever wrote them.
wrong_explanations.C: The extent of follow-up must consider each finding's significance (Standard 15.2); full retesting of every action spends effort the low-risk ones do not need.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 15.2 gives confirmation to internal auditors; reliance on another provider (Standard 9.5) needs a documented basis, and nothing here shows one.

tips: Eliminate: C, because follow-up effort must follow each finding's significance and most here are low-rated, and D, because confirmation is internal auditors' job and no basis for reliance exists.
Final two: A beats B because Standard 15.2 covers management's action plans as well as internal auditors' recommendations; self-reporting leaves confirmation with management.
Exam cue: on CIA follow-up questions, management implements every action and internal auditors confirm every action from their engagements, by inquiry, risk-based assessment and tracking.

questions.subtopic: 3D4 Closing communication and report distribution. An error below the agreed criteria
questions.question: A ferry line's issued report misstates fleet size in its background; by board-agreed criteria, the error changes no result, action or legal position. Which view of the chief audit executive's duty is most accurate?

options.A: Required: corrected information, promptly, to every original recipient.
options.B: Required: corrected information to the board, which oversees the function.
options.C: Not required: this error does not reach the threshold of significance here.
options.D: Not required: errors in a report's background section need no correction.

questions.key_concept: Standard 11.4's correction duty covers significant errors or omissions, judged by criteria agreed with the board; an error below them triggers no reissue.
questions.pre_read: Check what triggers Standard 11.4 and who set the yardstick for significance before choosing who must hear of the error.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.4 requires the chief audit executive to get corrected facts quickly to every party that had the original when a significant error or omission turns up in a final communication, judged by criteria agreed with the board. Its considerations weigh legal or regulatory effects and changes to results or action plans. This error meets none, so the duty is not triggered. Correcting for every recipient, the closest choice, fits significant errors only.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: that is the duty for a significant error, but Standard 11.4 judges significance by criteria agreed with the board, and this error meets none of them.
wrong_explanations.B: Even a significant error is corrected for every party who received the original, not for the board alone (Standard 11.4); here no correction is required at all.
wrong_explanations.D: The verdict fits, the reason does not: the board-agreed criteria decide significance (Standard 11.4), and a background error that changed a result, action or legal position would need correcting.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a correction goes to every original recipient, not the board alone, and D, because the agreed criteria, not the section holding the error, decide significance.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 11.4 is triggered only by a significant error or omission, and the board-agreed criteria place this one below the line.

Exam cue: on CIA correction questions, test significance against the criteria agreed with the board first; if significant, correct promptly for every original recipient; if not, Standard 11.4 is not triggered.

questions.subtopic: 3D2 Writing the final engagement communication. A second set of requirements beside the Standards
questions.question: A bank's engagement followed the Standards and the central bank's internal audit rules; supervision and quality results support conformance with both. What should its final communication, approved by the chief audit executive, best state?

options.A: Conformance with the central bank's rules, in place of the Standards.
options.B: Conformance with the Standards, and a citation of the central bank's rules.
options.C: Conformance with the Standards, with the central bank's rules cited on request.
options.D: No conformance statement, as one is only a consideration.

questions.key_concept: Another body's requirements used with the Standards must be cited in communications; the conformance statement is included where supervision and quality results support it.
questions.pre_read: Separate the conformance statement, a should backed by evidence, from what Standard 4.1 requires when another body's rules also apply.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 15.1's considerations say a statement of conformance with the Standards should be included when supervision and the quality program back it, as both do here. Standard 4.1 then requires something more: any communication from work that also followed another authority's rules must name those rules, as appropriate. Citing the central bank's rules only when someone asks, the closest choice, leaves readers of the report unaware of them.

wrong_explanations.A: Another body's rules sit beside the Standards, never in their place; the statement of conformance with the Standards stays where supervision and quality results support it (Standards 15.1, 4.1).
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the conformance statement is right, but Standard 4.1 requires communications to cite other requirements used with the Standards; holding them back until asked does not do that.
wrong_explanations.D: The statement is a should, but here supervision and quality results support it, and Standard 4.1 still requires citing the central bank's rules, a must that dropping every statement misses.

tips: Eliminate: A, because another body's rules never replace the Standards, and D, because the citation of the central bank's rules is a must even where a should is skipped.
Final two: B beats C because Standard 4.1 requires communications to cite another body's requirements used alongside the Standards; waiting for a request does not meet it.
Exam cue: on CIA conformance statement questions, the statement is a should backed by supervision and quality results; citing other bodies' requirements that were also followed is a must.
